Loyalty buyers have different seniority levels depending on the organization,
but they are all focused on acquiring and retaining customers and growing
lifetime value.
C-suite leaders often handle loyalty as part of overall brand marketing and
customer experience, so they are thinking about the “big picture” and what
their org needs to do to drive growth and support customer experiences
across channels. Those on the technical side are typically looking for
platform/SaaS solutions to enable these experiences seamlessly within the
brand’s tech stack. Senior leaders think more about loyalty as part of the
overall CX, vs as a “program.” They are budget owners for larger investments
like instantiating a loyalty program, investing in a SaaS platform, and retaining
agency services.
Director-level leaders are involved in the day-to-day of managing loyalty
programs and related campaigns/initiatives, so they are thinking about the
customer experience, but they are also more closely tied into the
performance of the program, delivering experiences that will drive their KPIs,
working with vendors they can gain loyalty expertise from, and managing the
performance of offers, rewards, promotions, etc.. They are sometimes budget
owners at the campaign level, so can fund a specific offer or rewards.

04
The Empowering of AI with First -Party Data
Current marketing and customer experience trends center on Personalization, AI -driven
insights, and the strategic use of first -party data. With digital signals and identifiers, including
Third -party cookies, businesses rely more on first -party data collected from direct customer
interactions. This shift allows for more personalized and privacy -compliant marketing,
enabling brands to tailor experiences across digital channels.
AI plays a pivotal role in transforming first -party data into actionable insights. Marketers can
now deliver real -time, hyper -personalized experiences at scale through the power of
machine learning and predictive analytics. AI's ability to identify patterns and customer
behaviors is driving better segmentation and targeting, opening up a world of possibilities
for personalized marketing.
While Customer Data Platforms (CDPs) are essential for activating this data and storing the
unified customer profiles, they are not a silver bullet. More than a CDP is needed to address
the complexities of managing and processing data from multiple sources. This is where data
engineering becomes vital —ensuring data is appropriately collected, cleaned, and
integrated into workflows. Without solid data pipelines, even advanced AI models and CDPs
can produce flawed insights, undermining marketing efforts.
Data engineering is the backbone that enables seamless integration across marketing tools,
ensuring that high -quality, accurate data fuels AI and personalization strategies. This
emphasis on data engineering should reassure businesses that their data is reliable and can
be trusted to drive their marketing success.
QUESTIONS TO ASK
• First-Party Data Strategy: "As reliance on third -party data fades, how
are you adapting your strategy to collect and leverage first -party data
from your customers?"
• AI and Personalization: "How are you using AI and machine learning
to create personalized experiences for your customers, and what
challenges are you facing?"
• Customer Data Platform (CDP) Use: "Are you currently using a
Customer Data Platform (CDP), and if so, are you finding it effective in
integrating all your customer data sources?"
• Data Engineering and Integration: "How confident are you in the
accuracy and quality of your data, and what steps have you taken to
ensure that your data pipelines are robust?"
• Privacy and Compliance: "With increasing privacy regulations, how
are you ensuring compliance while delivering personalized
experiences that drive customer engagement?"

TREND 2 NARRATIVE
04
Move to Composable Customer Data Platforms (CDPs)
Composable Customer Data Platforms (CDPs) are rapidly gaining traction as a flexible alternative to traditional,
monolithic CDPs. Unlike pre -packaged CDPs, composable CDPs allow businesses to build a modular data
infrastructure, integrating best -of-breed components for data collection, processing, and activation. This approach
provides greater customization and scalability, enabling organizations to adapt to their specific needs and evolving
martech landscapes.
In 2025, businesses should expect further advancement in composable CDPs, focusing more on real -time data
processing, AI -driven insights, and seamless platform integration. The flexibility of a composable stack allows
marketers to adopt emerging technologies without overhauling their entire system. However, this also increases
complexity, requiring strong data engineering and governance practices to ensure data quality, consistency, and
privacy compliance.
As brands prepare for 2025, they should focus on several key areas:
1. Data Integration: With the rise of composable CDPs, ensuring smooth and efficient data integration across different
components will be essential.
2. Real -time Capabilities: Customers increasingly expect real -time Personalization, so businesses must be able to
activate data instantly across channels.
3. AI and Automation: Leveraging AI to process and activate data will become critical for optimizing customer
experiences at scale. AI can be used to analyze large volumes of data, identify patterns, and predict customer
behavior, enabling businesses to deliver personalized experiences in real -time. This level of automation is essential
for keeping up with customer expectations and market trends.
4. Privacy and Compliance: As regulations evolve, composable CDPs must include built -in compliance mechanisms to
securely manage consent and data privacy.
Ultimately, a composable approach offers more agility, but businesses must invest in data engineering and AI to fully
realize its potential by 2025.

supporting that?"

that your current CDP setup can handle evolving
compliance needs without slowing down your
marketing efforts?"

TREND 3 NARRATIVE
04
Clean rooms maximize media spend insights while ensuring privacy
Clean rooms will be a critical tool for brands and agencies looking to gain deeper insights
into the effectiveness of their media spend. Clean rooms are secure, privacy -compliant
environments where first -party data from brands can be combined with aggregated data
from media platforms (such as Google, Facebook, or retail media networks) without directly
sharing sensitive information. As third -party cookies disappear and data privacy regulations
grow more stringent, clean rooms provide a solution that allows marketers to measure their
media campaigns' true impact while respecting user privacy.
One key advantage of clean rooms is the ability to perform multi -platform attribution. Since
clean rooms allow data from different sources to match without revealing individual
identities, brands can better understand how their media investments across different
platforms contribute to conversions and sales. This offers a clearer picture of which media
channels and campaigns are driving the most value.
Additionally, clean rooms enable deeper audience insights. By securely combining customer
data with anonymized platform data, marketers can refine targeting strategies, optimize
messaging, and personalize media campaigns in ways that were not possible before.
To fully leverage clean rooms, brands must ensure they have a robust data strategy in place,
with clean, well -governed first -party data ready for integration. In 2025, clean rooms will be
indispensable for any brand serious about maximizing media spend ROI while navigating an
increasingly privacy -conscious environment. Brands that invest in this technology will
optimize their marketing performance and drive business growth.
QUESTIONS TO ASK
• Media Attribution: "How confident are you in understanding which
media channels drive the most conversions for your campaigns?"
• Cross -Platform Measurement: "Do you struggle with tracking media
effectiveness across multiple platforms while maintaining customer
privacy?"
• Data Privacy and Compliance: "How are you handling data privacy
and compliance in your current media measurement and analytics
practices?"
• First -Party Data Utilization: "Are you fully leveraging your first -party
data to optimize media targeting and performance across various
advertising platforms?"
• Multi-Platform Insights: "Would you benefit from a secure, privacy -
compliant way to combine data from platforms like Google,
Facebook, and retail media networks to gain deeper insights into
media effectiveness?"

Different Types of Gamification
Gamification comes in many different forms, from the more traditional "game“ format to more subtle habit -driving mechanics. The first question is determining
which type of behavior you’re trying to drive and for what time period, which then can inform a more focused approach.
Implicit Gamification Is Ideal
for Ongoing Engagement
Looking for an always -on or evergreen solution to
change or sustain engagement or habits? Implicit
gamification is the use of gamification mechanics in
a less obvious way and is ideal for motivating
behavior over a longer duration. It is often used to
incentivize purchase, trial, and stretch behaviors
with ongoing offers that are evolving over time.
Explicit Gamification Is Ideal
for Pulsed Engagement
Explicit gamification is what most people think of
when they think gamification. Shorter -duration
gamified promotions can drive acquisition,
engagement, and behavior over a set window, using
more traditional game mechanics to inspire
purchases, education, social interaction, and more.

need to be delivered in non-traditional non-sequential journeys
and provide consumers increasingly personalized experiences,
while brands acquire more first-party data via engagement.

+  As the size of your email list
grows, it considerably increases
the cost of email marketing.
+  Removal of inactive or invalid
email addresses and
maintaining email list hygiene
can help you cut down on the
marketing expenses.
P R O G RAM CO S T
+  Having a poor-quality email list
can hamper your email
reputation.
+  Unless the subscribers receive
your email in their inbox, your
email strategy will be futile.
+  A bad reputation can deter your
engagement with subscribers
and affect the conversion rate as
well
R E P UT A T I ON
+  ISPs keep a close eye on email
senders who use spam traps to
reach the subscribers.
+  These spam traps are, in fact,
email addresses owned by ISPs
and the blacklist providers in
order to check that the email
marketers are abiding by the
best practices.
S P AM T R AP S
List Cleanse: Business Impact

PROPRIETARY AND CON FIDENTIAL
+  Misplaced or transposed @ signs
and invalid characters such as
spaces or quotes.
+  Typos in both TLD’s (.com, .net,
.edu, etc.) and LLD’s (gmail, aol,
Hotmail, etc.)
+  ANY misspelled domain, not just
the most popular ones.
+  Uncommon domain entries
(such as @google.com instead of
@gmail.com).
C O R R ECT
+  Determine whether the address
syntax conforms to RFC and
FreshAddress standards.
+  Confirm that domains and MX
records are valid and can accept
mail.
+  Ensure address meets ISP-
specific requirements.
+  Verify the account is linked to an
actual working mailbox.
C H E CK
+  Toxic: Spamtraps and honeypots
+  Undesirable: Frequent
complainers, role accounts,
disposable domains, fictitious
and malicious email addresses,
client-specific suppressions.
+  Not best-practice: DMA “Do Not
Email List” and FCC wireless
domains
